```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", fig.pos = "H")
```

```{r packages}
# 0. Packages: rpart fits CART trees, rpart.plot draws them
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
```

```{r data}
# 1. Load the data (data frame `data`: 4,000 customers, 13 variables)
load("Churn.RData")
churn.rate <- mean(data$Churn == "Yes")            # overall churn rate (37.5%)
```

```{r split}
# 2. Split 70/30 into training and test set; the seed makes the split reproducible
set.seed(123)
idx   <- sample(nrow(data), 0.7 * nrow(data))
train <- data[idx, ]
test  <- data[-idx, ]
```

```{r grow}
# 3. Grow the full tree on the training set: cp = 0 switches off pruning,
#    xval = 10 stores the 10-fold cross-validated error for every cp value
full <- rpart(Churn ~ ., data = train, method = "class",
              control = rpart.control(cp = 0, xval = 10))
```

```{r tune}
# 4. Tune cp with the 1-SE rule: smallest tree whose CV error (xerror) is
#    within one standard error (xstd) of the minimum CV error
cpt    <- full$cptable
best   <- cpt[which.min(cpt[, "xerror"]), ]
row1se <- which(cpt[, "xerror"] <= best["xerror"] + best["xstd"])[1]
cp.1se <- cpt[row1se, "CP"]
```

```{r prune}
# 5. Prune the full tree back to the chosen cp; variable importance in %
tree <- prune(full, cp = cp.1se)
imp  <- round(100 * tree$variable.importance / sum(tree$variable.importance), 1)
```

```{r predict}
# 6. Predict the test set (majority class of the leaf, i.e. cut-off 0.5)
#    and evaluate out-of-sample performance
pred <- predict(tree, test, type = "class")
cm   <- table(Predicted = pred, Actual = test$Churn)
acc  <- mean(pred == test$Churn)
sens <- cm["Yes", "Yes"] / sum(cm[, "Yes"])
spec <- cm["No", "No"]   / sum(cm[, "No"])
base <- mean(test$Churn == "No")                   # accuracy of always predicting "No"
acc.train <- mean(predict(tree, train, type = "class") == train$Churn)
acc.full  <- mean(predict(full, test, type = "class") == test$Churn)
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x)
```

# 1. Introduction

Customer churn (customers ending their contract and leaving for a competitor) is costly for telecom providers: acquiring a new customer costs more than retaining one, and customers become more profitable the longer they stay (Gupta et al., 2006). A telecom provider has therefore asked us to analyse the churn behaviour of `r format(nrow(data), big.mark = ",")` of its customers. Because the provider wants insight into *why* customers leave, not just a black-box prediction, we use a **classification tree**, which predicts churn with transparent if-then rules that managers can act on (James et al., 2013; Yildirim & Kübler, 2023). We grow and tune the tree on a training set and assess its predictions on a separate test set.

# 2. Data

For each customer we observe *Churn* (yes/no; `r format(sum(data$Churn == "Yes"), big.mark = ",")` customers or `r pct(churn.rate)` churned) and twelve predictors without missing values: contract term (*Contract*; 59.7% month-to-month), *tenure* (1--72 months), *MonthlyCharges* (\$18--\$119), *TotalCharges*, *Partner*, *PhoneService*, *MultipleLines*, *InternetService* (DSL, fibre optic or none) and four add-ons (*OnlineSecurity*, *OnlineBackup*, *DeviceProtection*, *TechSupport*), which take the value "No internet service" for the 19.4% of customers without internet. We randomly split the data (seed 123) into a **training set of `r format(nrow(train), big.mark = ",")` (70%)** and a **test set of `r format(nrow(test), big.mark = ",")` customers (30%)**, with similar churn rates (`r pct(mean(train$Churn == "Yes"))` and `r pct(mean(test$Churn == "Yes"))`). Always predicting "no churn" gives a baseline test accuracy of `r pct(base)`.

# 3. Methods

**Decision trees.** A classification tree splits customers into groups by asking a sequence of yes/no questions about their attributes (e.g. "Is the contract month-to-month?"). Each final group (*leaf*) predicts its majority class, and its share of churners is an estimated churn probability (Tan et al., 2014). We fit the tree with the CART algorithm (Breiman et al., 1984) in the R package `rpart` (Therneau & Atkinson, 2023). The tree is grown top-down by *recursive binary splitting*: at each node every predictor and cut-point (or grouping of categories) is tried, and the split that most reduces the Gini impurity $G = 1 - \sum_k \hat p_k^2$ is chosen (James et al., 2013). This search is greedy, i.e. a split is never revised later.

**The complexity parameter.** A fully grown tree fits noise in the training data and generalises poorly (overfitting). CART therefore prunes the tree by minimising $R_{cp}(T) = R(T) + cp \cdot |T| \cdot R(T_{\text{root}})$, where $R(T)$ is the training misclassification error, $|T|$ the number of leaves and $R(T_{\text{root}})$ the error without splits. The **complexity parameter** $cp$ is the price of an extra leaf: a split is kept only if it lowers the relative error by at least $cp$. $cp = 0$ gives the full tree; larger values give smaller trees.

**Tuning.** We grow the full tree ($cp = 0$) and let `rpart` estimate the out-of-sample error of every pruned subtree with **10-fold cross-validation** (*xerror*, with standard error *xstd*). We choose $cp$ with the **one-standard-error (1-SE) rule**: the simplest tree whose xerror is within one standard error of the minimum (Hastie et al., 2009). This yields a more interpretable tree whose accuracy is statistically indistinguishable from the best one. Test customers are classified as churners if their leaf's churn probability exceeds 0.5.

# 4. Results

**Tuning.** The full tree has `r max(cpt[, "nsplit"])` splits and a cross-validated relative error of `r sprintf("%.3f", cpt[nrow(cpt), "xerror"])`. The error is lowest (`r sprintf("%.3f", best["xerror"])`) at `r best["nsplit"]` splits; larger trees fit noise (Appendix A, Table A1). The 1-SE rule selects $cp$ = `r sprintf("%.4f", cp.1se)`: a tree with **`r cpt[row1se, "nsplit"]` splits and `r cpt[row1se, "nsplit"] + 1` leaves** (xerror `r sprintf("%.3f", cpt[row1se, "xerror"])`, Figure 1).

```{r tree-plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=3.4, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Pruned tree. Each node shows the predicted class, the churn probability and the share of training customers."}
rpart.plot(tree, type = 2, extra = 106, under = TRUE, box.palette = "GnRd",
           fallen.leaves = TRUE, cex = 0.7)
```

**Interpretation.** *Contract* is the root split and the most important variable (`r imp["Contract"]`% of importance), followed by *tenure* (`r imp["tenure"]`%), *TotalCharges* (`r imp["TotalCharges"]`%), *TechSupport* (`r imp["TechSupport"]`%) and *OnlineSecurity* (`r imp["OnlineSecurity"]`%). The main rules are:

1. **One- or two-year contracts:** 41% of customers, only 11% churn.
2. **Month-to-month, fibre optic, tenure under 17 months:** the highest-risk group (19% of customers, 82% churn).
3. **Month-to-month fibre customers with longer tenure** churn at 35% with online security. Without it, those paying at least \$74.28 per month churn at 59% without tech support, against 41% with it.
4. **Month-to-month DSL or no internet:** 29% churn after 6 months' tenure, but 64% for newer customers without online security.

**Test-set performance.** The pruned tree classifies **`r pct(acc)`** of the `r format(nrow(test), big.mark = ",")` test customers correctly, against the `r pct(base)` baseline. Its training accuracy (`r pct(acc.train)`) is similar, so it generalises well, while the unpruned tree reaches only `r pct(acc.full)`. It detects **`r pct(sens)`** of churners (sensitivity; `r cm["Yes", "Yes"]` of `r sum(cm[, "Yes"])`) and correctly clears **`r pct(spec)`** of non-churners (specificity; `r cm["No", "No"]` of `r sum(cm[, "No"])`). Of the `r sum(cm["Yes", ])` customers it flags, `r pct(cm["Yes", "Yes"] / sum(cm["Yes", ]))` actually churn.

# 5. Conclusions and Discussion

A pruned nine-leaf tree predicts churn of unseen customers with `r pct(acc)` accuracy (baseline `r pct(base)`). Churn is driven mainly by **commitment** (contract), **customer lifetime** (tenure) and the **service bundle** (fibre internet, online security and tech support). This suggests three actions: (1) encourage month-to-month customers (56% churn) to move to longer contracts (11%); (2) prioritise new fibre-optic customers (82% churn) with onboarding support and a review of fibre pricing and quality; and (3) offer online security and tech support at a discount, as customers with these add-ons churn less.

**Limitations.** The tree misses `r pct(1 - sens)` of churners; a lower probability cut-off would catch more at the cost of more false alarms. Single trees are unstable, so the exact cut-points (e.g. 16.5 months) are approximate. Finally, the rules show associations, not causes; a controlled retention campaign should test whether the proposed actions actually reduce churn.

# Appendix A: Tables

**Table A1.** Cost-complexity table of the full tree (selected rows, 10-fold cross-validation). Errors are relative to the root-node error; the 1-SE rule selects $cp$ = `r sprintf("%.4f", cp.1se)` (8 splits).

```{r cptable}
keep <- cpt[, "nsplit"] %in% c(0:4, 6, 8, 10, 20, best["nsplit"], max(cpt[, "nsplit"]))
tab  <- data.frame(cp = sprintf("%.4f", cpt[keep, "CP"]), Splits = cpt[keep, "nsplit"],
                   Leaves = cpt[keep, "nsplit"] + 1,
                   round(cpt[keep, c("rel error", "xerror", "xstd")], 3))
names(tab)[4:6] <- c("Training error", "CV error", "CV std. error")
knitr::kable(tab, row.names = FALSE)
```

**Table A2.** Relative variable importance in the pruned tree (% of total; includes surrogate splits).

```{r importance}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Variable = names(imp), `Importance (%)` = imp, check.names = FALSE),
             row.names = FALSE)
```

# 7. Figure 1 and test-set results: plot the pruned tree, print the confusion matrix
rpart.plot(tree, type = 2, extra = 106, under = TRUE, box.palette = "GnRd",
           fallen.leaves = TRUE, cex = 0.7)
cm; c(accuracy = acc, sensitivity = sens, specificity = spec, baseline = base)
